summary: This informational document describes a well-known BGP community called BLACKHOLE for destination-based blackholing in IP networks. An origin AS can use it to ask a neighboring network to discard traffic destined to the tagged prefix, which is often used to limit damage from a denial-of-service attack.

plainLanguage.summary: When a street is flooded with unwanted traffic, you can block it off. This defines a standard flag a network can attach to ask its neighbors to throw away traffic heading to a victim.

subtitle: A standard BGP community to signal that traffic to an IP prefix should be discarded.

tldr.problem: When networks suffer DDoS attacks, they need a way to ask neighboring networks to discard traffic headed to the victim. Different networks use different mechanisms, making this cumbersome and error-prone.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7999 defines a well-known BGP community called BLACKHOLE (value 0xFFFF029A) that an origin network can attach to an IP prefix announcement to signal: 'please discard all traffic destined to this prefix.'
tldr.outcome: Networks can now use a standard, uniform mechanism for blackholing, simplifying operations and reducing the need for custom configuration or out-of-band coordination during attacks.

today: RFC 7999 is Informational and has become the standard specification for the BLACKHOLE BGP community. It has not been obsoleted or updated. Many networks now recognize and support this community, though deployment remains voluntary and requires explicit operator configuration.

sections.title: The Problem: Too Many Blackholing Mechanisms
sections.content:
DDoS attacks flood networks with unwanted traffic. A common defense is to announce that traffic destined to a victim IP address should be discarded entirely, a technique called blackholing.

The problem: different networks have historically used different methods to signal this. Some use predefined next-hop IP addresses, others use BGP communities (special attributes that carry metadata about routes), and still others require out-of-band agreements or special BGP sessions. This patchwork makes network operations unnecessarily complex and error-prone, especially during an active attack when speed matters.

RFC 7999 solves this by defining a single well-known BGP community that all networks can recognize and understand. A network under attack can announce its victim IP prefix with this community attached, and neighboring networks that support it will automatically discard the traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: Before this, each network had its own way of saying 'drop this traffic.' Now there is one standard signal everyone understands.

sections.title: The BLACKHOLE Community
sections.content:
The BLACKHOLE community is a well-known BGP transitive community. In BGP terminology, 'transitive' means the community travels along with the route announcement as it propagates from network to network.

The community value is 0xFFFF029A (expressed in hexadecimal). In decimal, the low-order two octets are 666—a number long associated with blackholing in network operator culture.

When a network announces an IP prefix and attaches the BLACKHOLE community to it, it is signaling: 'Traffic destined to this prefix should be discarded.' The semantics are advisory—neighboring networks can choose to honor the community or ignore it.

The community is most useful when combined with destination-based blackholing, where a network operator announces a highly specific IP prefix (often a single host, /32 for IPv4 or /128 for IPv6) covering only the victim, minimizing collateral damage to other traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of it as a label on a route announcement that says 'discard this.' Networks that see the label can drop traffic to that destination.

sections.title: How to Use BLACKHOLE Safely
sections.content:
RFC 7999 provides operational guidance for using the BLACKHOLE community responsibly.

First, bilateral peering relationships: if two networks peer directly, they should agree in advance that they will respect the BLACKHOLE community. It is not automatic; operators must explicitly configure their routers to honor it.

Second, multilateral peering (route servers): if a network participates in a shared route server (a central point where many networks exchange routes), operators should follow the route server's policy on BLACKHOLE communities.

Third, preventing leaks: when a network receives a BLACKHOLE-tagged prefix, it should add the NO_ADVERTISE or NO_EXPORT community to prevent the prefix from leaking outside the local AS. Accidentally announcing a more specific blackhole prefix to the public Internet can cause serious harm.

Fourth, prefix length limits: the RFC notes that routes longer than /24 (IPv4) or /48 (IPv6) are generally not accepted on the Internet. For blackholing to work, the blackhole prefix should be as specific as possible (/32 or /128), which requires special handling and explicit bilateral agreements.

Finally, authorization: receiving networks should verify that the announcing network is actually authorized to advertise the prefix before honoring the blackhole. For example, an attacker might try to announce example.com's IP space with BLACKHOLE attached to knock them offline.
sections.plainLanguage: Just like a stop sign only works if everyone agrees to follow it, BLACKHOLE only works when both networks have agreed to respect it. You must also be careful not to accidentally block someone else's legitimate traffic.

sections.title: Security Implications and Validation
sections.content:
The BLACKHOLE community creates potential security risks if misused. An attacker could announce an IP prefix with BLACKHOLE attached to cause a network operator's legitimate traffic to be discarded across the Internet.

To mitigate this risk, RFC 7999 emphasizes strong validation: a receiving network must verify that the announcing network is actually authorized to advertise the prefix. This typically means using BGP route filtering and origin validation techniques such as BGP Prefix Origin Validation (ROV), which ensures that only the legitimate originating AS can announce a prefix.

Additionally, operators should only honor BLACKHOLE from trusted peers with bilateral agreements. Networks should implement strict prefix filtering, checking that announced prefixes match what the peer is authorized to advertise.

Note that once a BLACKHOLE community is attached to a prefix, that information should be protected from unauthorized modification during transit. Operators are encouraged to store all BGP updates carrying BLACKHOLE for long-term auditing and forensic analysis.
sections.plainLanguage: A bad actor could misuse this signal to knock a legitimate network offline, so you must verify that whoever is announcing the blackhole prefix actually owns it and is allowed to.

left.title: Before (Fragmented)
left.desc: Each network used its own custom mechanism (predefined IP, special session, or private communities).

right.title: After (Standard)
right.desc: Use the well-known BLACKHOLE community (0xFFFF029A) with any standard BGP session.
